page.home.title: Living Cultural Corridors
page.home.hero.title: Culture lives in relationships
page.home.hero.body: Human cultures do not live only in monuments, museums, archives or officially designated heritage sites. They live in relationships — in the ways people move, eat, work, trade, remember, make things, inhabit landscapes, care for places, tell stories, use water, cultivate land, build settlements, welcome strangers, adapt to environmental change, and imagine the future.
page.home.intro.title: The project
page.home.intro.body: This field-based, comparative and digitally enabled project investigates how human cultural relations persist, transform and regenerate through movement, place, material life, environment and networks of exchange. The Beijing Grand Canal is the primary field laboratory, Gotland the principal Swedish comparison, with focused studies in Southern Öland and Linköping.
page.home.vision.title: The deeper ambition
page.home.vision.body: How do human communities carry meaningful relationships from the past into viable futures, while allowing culture itself to change?
page.home.lens.title: The spotting lens
page.home.lens.body: A particular analytical lens runs through the Beijing case: the subtle interfaces between the Grand Canal and wider Silk Roads systems of movement and exchange.
page.corridors.title: Living Cultural Corridors
page.corridors.intro.title: Research corridors
page.corridors.intro.body: A corridor is more than a physical route. A canal, road, river, maritime passage, railway or trade path can become a medium through which people, goods, knowledge, technologies, foods, memories, skills and ways of living encounter one another. But the corridor itself is not the culture — culture emerges through the relationships that develop around it.
page.corridors.comparison.title: The comparative architecture
page.corridors.comparison.body: Two cases, one broader phenomenon: how can a place be deeply connected to distant worlds without becoming culturally indistinguishable from them? Beijing and Gotland are treated as different examples of local cultural worlds embedded in extensive networks of exchange.
page.scholars.title: Scholars
page.scholars.intro.title: Theoretical constellation
page.scholars.intro.body: The project works with a constellation of thinkers whose work grounds its epistemology of movement, place, materiality, heritage and regeneration.
page.literature.title: Literature Review
page.literature.intro.title: The review as groundwork
page.literature.intro.body: This page is the project's reading groundwork: a verified, annotated review of the scholars whose work gives the project its premises about movement, place, material life, heritage and regeneration. It is designed to be a living reference — the basis for ongoing brainstorming, the combing of ideas and viewpoints, and the transition into substantive research. The companion document (materials/LITERATURE_REVIEW.md) carries the full annotated bibliography, keyed to the mapping of each source to the research questions.
page.literature.synthesis.title: A synthesis in six dimensions
page.literature.synthesis.body: The review organises every involved scholar through six dimensions. Premises: things act; walking makes knowledge; heritage works for future generations; change is the baseline. Perspectives: four analytical lenses — walking/movement, materiality/things/ruins, heritage futures, and connectivity/corridors. Ethos: embrace change, befriend decay, respect local livelihoods, answer to future generations. Method: the three-walk method, following one thing, food-tracing, island comparison, digital ethnography, narrative policy analysis. Practice: field cycles in Beijing, Gotland and Southern Öland, with regeneration observation. Persona: each scholar's academic taste, quality, spirit, character, concerns and philosophy — read from their verified works and positions.
page.literature.portraits_note.title: How to read the portraits
page.literature.portraits_note.body: The portraits below are academic persona sketches [project reading], derived from each scholar's verified works and institutional positions — never from private life or speculation. Each portrait carries six dimensions: taste (what they are drawn to), quality (scholarly strengths), spirit (working stance), character (temperament), concerns (what keeps them up at night), and philosophy (their deeper commitments). Selected works are prioritised by relevance to this project and source-labelled [A] primary / [B] authoritative secondary.
page.literature.extended.title: Extended circle
page.literature.extended.body: Around the five core scholars sits an extended circle of verified collaborators and co-authors: Þóra Pétursdóttir (Ruin Memories; Theory Adrift with Olsen), Caitlin DeSilvey (Curated Decay; palliative curation), Sharon Macdonald (Memorylands; Heritage Futures), Rodney Harrison (Heritage: Critical Approaches; Heritage Futures editor), Anders Högberg (Cultural Heritage and the Future with Holtorf; 'No future in archaeological heritage management?'), Jo Vergunst (Ways of Walking with Ingold), Gustav Wollentz and Samantha May (co-authors on heritage-futures), the Shanks–Webmoor–Witmore triangle (Archaeology: The Discipline of Things), the Gotland–Rapa Nui team of Poort, Persson-Fischier, Elf Donaldson and Schaub, and Gillette's co-authors Emma Boyd, Elizabeth Bennett and Milena Arias Schreiber.
page.literature.verification.title: Verification & open items
page.literature.verification.body: Every citation on this page has been web-verified, and sources are labelled [A] primary / [B] authoritative secondary / [C] general / [D] unverified clue. Known corrections and open items include: Gillette's mining-heritage article is 2024 (Journal of Heritage Tourism 19(1)) with E. Boyd — not 2023; the 2026 Sociologia Ruralis herring-quota paper is verified via Wiley DOI 10.1111/soru.70050, but co-authorship with Singleton is not verified [D]; Ingold's Imagining for Real is treated as Routledge 2022 / openedition 2021; the Ruin Memories project (NRC 2009–2013) and Arctic Silk Road engagement are recorded as project-type entries. Ridanäs UNESCO status, Kinda Canal liveness and Öland UNESCO Ref 968 boundaries remain open items to be checked before any published claim.
page.methodology.title: Methodology
page.methodology.field.title: Let the field change the researcher
page.methodology.field.body: Before entering a field site, record: What do I expect? During fieldwork: What do I actually observe? Afterward: What was wrong or incomplete in my original understanding? The field notebook thus contains three explicit categories — EXPECTED, OBSERVED, REVISED — and one more: SURPRISE.
page.methodology.walk.title: The three-walk method
page.methodology.walk.body: Walk A — the researcher's walk, alone. Walk B — the local walk, with a resident or long-term participant asking 'What matters here?'. Walk C — the practitioner walk, with someone working in heritage, tourism, food, archaeology, museums or local government asking 'What do outsiders misunderstand?'. The differences among these walks become data.
page.methodology.follow.title: Following one thing
page.methodology.follow.body: At each field site, choose one tangible thing and follow it — grain, fish, vegetables, ceramics, brick, salt, textiles, a craft, a food. Do not begin by asking what the object means. First ask: Where does it come from? Where does it go? Who touches it? Where does its mode of transport change? Who gives it meaning?
page.methodology.food.title: Following food
page.methodology.food.body: Food is one of the strongest cross-scale tracers. A food item can connect: soil/water → production → farmer → road → canal → market → city → household/restaurant → memory/identity → tourism → future sustainability. This links naturally to regenerative heritage work on Öland, where archaeological soil, plants and food explore how the past can generate new life.
page.methodology.five.title: Scope discipline
page.methodology.five.body: The Grand Canal–Silk Roads relationship: a spotting lens, not a separate giant historical programme. Food: a tracer of relationships, not an independent discipline. Tourism: a revealing contemporary context, not the main subject. AI: a research instrument, not the project's identity.
page.fieldwork.title: Fieldwork
page.fieldwork.c1.title: Cycle 1 — Beijing immersion
page.fieldwork.c1.body: 7–14 days exploring Shichahai–Yuhe, Tongzhou, Zhangjiawan and the canal gateway environments. Following the canal–Silk Roads lens in the field: what arrives, what leaves, where transfer occurs, what changes, what remains after the route changes.
page.fieldwork.c2.title: Cycle 2 — Gotland
page.fieldwork.c2.body: 7–10 days comparing the Baltic island context — Visby's Hanseatic past, Ridanäs's trading connections, rural and coastal Gotland.
page.fieldwork.c3.title: Cycle 3 — Southern Öland
page.fieldwork.c3.body: 3–5 days at the regeneration laboratory — Gamla Skogsby's Iron Age evidence and the question of when the past becomes capable of generating future life.
page.fieldwork.c4.title: Cycle 4 — Linköping
page.fieldwork.c4.body: 3–5 days on the Kinda–Göta canal landscape — what happens to cultural meaning when an infrastructure loses its original economic function.
page.fieldwork.c5.title: Cycle 5 — Return to Beijing
page.fieldwork.c5.body: The logic is circular: BEIJING → SURPRISE → SWEDISH COMPARISON → REVISED THEORY → RETURN TO BEIJING → TEST. The goal is a research practice in which the world can force the theory to change.
page.graph.title: Knowledge Graph
page.graph.intro.title: Graph as infrastructure
page.graph.intro.body: This page renders the project's knowledge graph directly from the database: corridors, heritage sites, scholars, and the relations among them. It is a management and maintenance surface — add, edit or delete nodes and edges in the data layer and this page updates automatically, with no code changes.
page.graph.rg.title: Corridor profiles
page.graph.rg.body: Each corridor carries its attached sites (belongs_to) and scholars (studies). Relations are stored in a dedicated edge table and resolved by locale at render time.
